definition: Trite means not original; worn out by everyone's overuse.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word trite. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know trite should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: By the fourth graduation speech, every 'chase your dreams' landed as trite as a fortune cookie.

Common is neutral census-taking — it counts how widely a phrase turns up, well short of trite: a phrase can be common and still do honest work, while trite says the overuse has already rubbed the surprise off.
Meaningless goes further than trite — a trite phrase still says something, tiredly; a meaningless one has been rubbed all the way down to noise.

Worn-out says the force is simply gone — used so often the words no longer move anyone, and no blame attached. Trite adds the accusation: everybody got there before you, and reaching for the phrase anyway was the lazy move. Worn-out describes the wear; trite condemns the choice.

Secondhand means borrowed rather than your own — the thinking was taken over from someone who got there first, whether one source or a hundred. Trite goes further: borrowed so often, by so many, that the freshness is gone. Secondhand faults the sourcing; trite faults the staleness too.

The wedding videographer keeps a private tally of trite shots couples request anyway: rings resting on rose petals, a slow-motion sparkler exit, hands forming a heart around the sunset.
None of it is wrong, she says — it's just that ten thousand couples reached the sunset first, and the freshness went with them.
Trite is the diagnosis because it means not original; overused — the shot still works mechanically, but repetition has rubbed all the surprise off it.
Stale says the freshness is gone; trite adds the judgment that everyone else got there first, and that reaching for it was the lazy move.
Trite condemns: the expression was everybody's before it was yours, and choosing it was the lazy move.
Stale mourns lost freshness without pointing fingers; corny faults cheap sentiment.
Fresh and original are what the editor wanted instead.

The slogan intern's first pitch — 'Quality you can trust' — came back with one word from the creative director: trite.
The intern protested that the line was clear, positive, and grammatically perfect.
All true, the director agreed, and beside the point: the phrase had been printed on cereal boxes, banks, and tire shops for fifty years, and every reader's eye now slides straight past it.
Worse, choosing it was the easy way out — the first phrase the mind reaches for is the one everyone else already used.
The intern's second pitch took three days.
Nobody's eye slid past it.
